--- title: "Sometimes interpretability doesn't cost predictive power" description: "This was one of those times" author: Mitch Henderson date: 2026-10-28 image: /img/nfl_short_pass_thumbnail.png format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 code-fold: true code-tools: true html-table-processing: none execute: echo: true warning: false message: false knitr: opts_chunk: dev: "ragg_png" --- ::: callout-note ## tl;dr A simple, interpretable model fit to features representing football concepts predicted as well as a neural network fit to player tracking data. ::: ## The inspo I came across a [sports analytics project shared online in 2025](https://medium.com/@lou.j.dimuro/predicting-nfl-short-pass-success-with-a-cnn-2f279c985769) by [Lou DiMuro](https://www.linkedin.com/in/lou-dimuro/) that I really liked. It uses NFL player tracking data from the start of the 2021 and 2022 seasons to estimate, for plays where the QB throws a completed short pass, the probability the play will be successful. A short pass here is one where the receiver is at most 2 yards past the line of scrimmage when the ball is released. It has an awesome GIF showing the players' movement as a play progresses with a live updating estimate (obviously inspired my video above). Very cool. What counts as a 'successful' play in their analysis depends on the down: - On **1st down**, the play needs to **gain ≥ 40%** of the yards needed for a new set of downs - On **2nd down**, it needs to **gain ≥ 60%** - On **3rd or 4th down**, it needs to **gain 100%** What's interesting is that the model needs to account for the yards a receiver might gain after the catch, which aren't known at the time of the pass. It's judged on the outcome of the entire play (not just the pass). Only completed passes are included (no incompletions or interceptions), so it's essentially asking "will the play gain enough yards assuming it's caught?" It uses a [convolutional](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KuXjwB4LzSA&t=87s) [neural network](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rEDzUT3ymw4) (CNN) to estimate the probability of a successful play at the moment the ball is released. A strength of CNNs is that they can learn patterns from complex, high-dimensional inputs (e.g., position and velocity of all 22 players on the field). This comes at the cost of some interpretability. They can be very good at recognising situations that make a pass more or less likely to succeed, but understanding why the likelihood changes or how much different aspects of the play contribute to it is hard. Whether interpretability like this matters depends on what we want from the model. If the main goal is pure prediction, giving a flexible model access to the full tracking data makes sense. But in applied sport environments, analysts also need to explain and discuss predictions with coaches or players who need to make decisions and actually do things in the game. Those conversations often turn to what might have happened if someone did something differently. A coach wants to know: > If I ask a player to instead do it *this* way, what can I expect to change? An athlete watching film might think: > If I do *this*, how might the defenders respond and how would that impact the play? These are causal questions that can't be answered from observational play data alone. What can be done though, is to represent the plays in football terms and examine how those representations relate to success. For example: > How does the space around a receiver at the time of the pass relate to the probability of a successful play? > > How does the nearest defender's closing speed relate to the chance of success? Putting the questions in football terms like this gives coaches and players something concrete to challenge. They might disagree with how I've represented space or closing speed conceptually, or whether the relationships found make sense to them based on their domain knowledge. That discussion might uncover something worth testing with a research design that can estimate a causal effect. My aim here is to turn the data used to train the CNN into a small set of domain-informed "football features" (e.g., space around a receiver, blocker positioning, etc) and use Bayesian [logistic regression](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yIYKR4sgzI8&t=343s) to model the probability of success. The features make my choices about how to represent the play explicit, the regression model makes the relationships easier to inspect, and the Bayesian approach lets me quantify and carry the uncertainty in those relationships through to the predicted probability of success. The question is whether the transparency gained by making those football concepts explicit costs much in predictive performance. ## The data :::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="R code · packages"} library(tidyverse) library(cmdstanr) library(posterior) library(bayesplot) library(ggdist) library(patchwork) library(ggtext) library(gt) library(SBC) register_knitr_engine() systemfonts::require_font("Poppins") data_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mitchhenderson/mitchhenderson.dev/main/posts/2026-10-19-nfl-interpretability-vs-predictive-power/data-public" ``` ::: ## ![Python](/img/python-logo-only.svg){height="30"} ::: callout-note ## Python code outputs will differ from rendered results The charts and tables on this page are made by the R code. The Python code runs the same analysis, but its charts are much simpler (no annotations or custom styling) and its tables use great_tables' defaults. R and Python also use different random number generators and samplers (Stan through CmdStanR in R, PyMC in Python), so the exact numbers won't match. The statistical results (the model's estimates, the cross-validated scores and the probabilities) should be the same within the noise of random sampling. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code code-summary="Python code · packages"} import itertools import math import tempfile import urllib.request import arviz as az import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import polars as pl import pymc as pm import rdata import xarray as xr from formulaic import model_matrix from great_tables import GT from scipy import stats from scipy.special import expit DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mitchhenderson/mitchhenderson.dev/main/posts/2026-10-19-nfl-interpretability-vs-predictive-power/data-public" NAVY = "#134A8E" PALE_NAVY = "#C4D2E3" RED = "#E31937" plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False}) ``` ::: :::: The raw tracking data comes from the [NFL's Next Gen Stats Big Data Bowl](https://operations.nfl.com/programs-initiatives/innovation/big-data-bowl). The data is available on [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com), split across two competitions. [Big Data Bowl 2023](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2023) contains data from weeks 1–8 of the 2021 season and [Big Data Bowl 2025](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2025) has weeks 1–9 of the 2022 season. With ~50 frames per play and the position of every player and ball recorded at each frame, the full tracking dataset is ~3.7M rows. You can download it with a free Kaggle account after joining each competition and accepting the rules. I didn't work directly from the raw Kaggle data. I used the preprocessed data from [Lou's project GitHub repo](https://github.com/ldimuro/NFL-Short-Pass-Success-Probability), which captures only the completed short pass plays and transforms the data into tensors suitable for modelling with a neural network. It includes 3,228 plays, and 59% of them were successful. Instead of re-publishing the full 100+ MB dataset, I've included one play in the reference repo's format as an example to demonstrate how I transformed it. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="R code · turning the reference format into tables"} example_play <- read_rds(file.path(data_url, "example_play_tensor.rds")) flatten_play_data <- function(tensors) { defender_rows <- expand_grid( play_row = seq_len(dim(tensors)[1]), defender_slot = seq_len(dim(tensors)[3]) ) |> mutate( # The reference format stores each velocity as (y, x), not (x, y) defender_velocity_x = tensors[ cbind(play_row, 2L, defender_slot, 1L) ], defender_velocity_y = tensors[ cbind(play_row, 1L, defender_slot, 1L) ], defender_offset_downfield = tensors[cbind( play_row, 3L, defender_slot, 1L )], defender_offset_lateral = tensors[ cbind(play_row, 4L, defender_slot, 1L) ], defender_velocity_relative_x = tensors[cbind( play_row, 6L, defender_slot, 1L )], defender_velocity_relative_y = tensors[cbind( play_row, 5L, defender_slot, 1L )] ) |> filter_out(defender_offset_downfield == 0, defender_offset_lateral == 0) blocker_rows <- expand_grid( play_row = seq_len(dim(tensors)[1]), defender_slot = seq_len(dim(tensors)[3]), offender_slot = seq_len(dim(tensors)[4]) ) |> semi_join(defender_rows, by = join_by(play_row, defender_slot)) |> mutate( offender_offset_downfield = tensors[cbind( play_row, 7L, defender_slot, offender_slot )], offender_offset_lateral = tensors[cbind( play_row, 8L, defender_slot, offender_slot )], offender_velocity_relative_downfield = tensors[cbind( play_row, 10L, defender_slot, offender_slot )], offender_velocity_relative_lateral = tensors[cbind( play_row, 9L, defender_slot, offender_slot )] ) |> filter_out(offender_offset_downfield == 0, offender_offset_lateral == 0) play_context <- tibble( play_row = seq_len(dim(tensors)[1]), down = tensors[, 11L, 1L, 1L] * 3, yards_to_go = tensors[, 12L, 1L, 1L] * 29.5 + 0.5 ) |> mutate( down = pmin(4L, pmax(1L, round(down))), # The yardage the play actually has to gain, given the down. yards_needed = recode_values(down, 1 ~ 0.4, 2 ~ 0.6, default = 1) * yards_to_go ) list( defenders = defender_rows, blockers = blocker_rows, context = play_context ) } tabular_play <- flatten_play_data(example_play) ``` ::: ## ![Python](/img/python-logo-only.svg){height="30"} ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code code-summary="Python code · turning the reference format into tables"} def read_rds(url): """An array saved from R as .rds, and its attributes.""" with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".rds") as file: urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, file.name) parsed = rdata.parser.parse_file(file.name) converter = rdata.conversion.SimpleConverter() return converter.convert(parsed.object), converter.convert(parsed.object.attributes) example_play, example_attributes = read_rds(f"{DATA_URL}/example_play_tensor.rds") def flatten_play_data(tensors): n_plays, _, n_defenders, n_offence = tensors.shape def both_zero(prefix): return (pl.col(f"{prefix}_offset_downfield") == 0) & ( pl.col(f"{prefix}_offset_lateral") == 0 ) play_row, defender_slot = np.meshgrid( np.arange(n_plays), np.arange(n_defenders), indexing="ij" ) def defender(channel): return tensors[:, channel, :, 0].ravel() defender_rows = pl.DataFrame( { "play_row": play_row.ravel(), "defender_slot": defender_slot.ravel(), # The reference format stores each velocity as (y, x), not (x, y) "defender_velocity_x": defender(1), "defender_velocity_y": defender(0), "defender_offset_downfield": defender(2), "defender_offset_lateral": defender(3), "defender_velocity_relative_x": defender(5), "defender_velocity_relative_y": defender(4), } ).filter(~both_zero("defender")) play_row, defender_slot, offender_slot = np.meshgrid( np.arange(n_plays), np.arange(n_defenders), np.arange(n_offence), indexing="ij" ) def offender(channel): return tensors[:, channel, :, :].ravel() blocker_rows = ( pl.DataFrame( { "play_row": play_row.ravel(), "defender_slot": defender_slot.ravel(), "offender_slot": offender_slot.ravel(), "offender_offset_downfield": offender(6), "offender_offset_lateral": offender(7), "offender_velocity_relative_downfield": offender(9), "offender_velocity_relative_lateral": offender(8), } ) .join( defender_rows.select("play_row", "defender_slot"), on=["play_row", "defender_slot"], how="semi", ) .filter(~both_zero("offender")) ) play_context = ( pl.DataFrame( { "play_row": np.arange(n_plays), "down": tensors[:, 10, 0, 0] * 3, "yards_to_go": tensors[:, 11, 0, 0] * 29.5 + 0.5, } ) .with_columns(down=pl.col("down").round().clip(1, 4).cast(pl.Int64)) .with_columns( # The yardage the play actually has to gain, given the down yards_needed=pl.col("down").replace_strict({1: 0.4, 2: 0.6}, default=1.0) * pl.col("yards_to_go") ) ) return { "defenders": defender_rows, "blockers": blocker_rows, "context": play_context, } tabular_play = flatten_play_data(example_play) ``` ::: ::: Here's that play at the moment of release. Instead of feeding the model every player's position and velocity directly, I define things that I think might matter (e.g., how far the nearest defender is from the receiver and how quickly they're closing that space). The data says where the receiver and defenders are, but I'm deciding which football concepts within those measurements might inform the outcome. Someone with a different view of the game might choose differently. That's a limitation, but it also puts the assumptions out in the open. The simplest example is yards needed. The CNN was given the down and distance and had to learn the success rule from the data. I already know the rule, so I just calculated the yards each play needs and gave the model that instead. The model I built uses nine features covering six concepts: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="R code · calculate and show the features"} # The features for every play in a set of tables from flatten_play_data(), # one row per play # receiver_depth comes separately from the season play data, not the tensors. # The line of scrimmage is at x = 60 after preprocessing, so receiver_depth # is the receiver's x position at release minus 60 (positive beyond the line). calculate_features <- function(tables) { defenders <- tables$defenders |> mutate( distance = sqrt(defender_offset_downfield^2 + defender_offset_lateral^2), # How fast the gap to the receiver is shrinking (positive is closing): # the relative velocity along the line between them closing_speed = -(defender_offset_downfield * defender_velocity_relative_x + defender_offset_lateral * defender_velocity_relative_y) / (distance + 1e-6) ) around_the_receiver <- defenders |> summarise( # The nearest defender in front of the receiver, or the farthest # defender if nobody is in front space_ahead = if (any(defender_offset_downfield > 0)) { min(distance[defender_offset_downfield > 0]) } else { max(distance) }, room_beyond_nearest = space_ahead - min(distance), min_def_y_distance_to_rec = min(abs(defender_offset_lateral)), nearest_def_cushion = defender_offset_downfield[which.min(distance)], def_y_spread = sd(defender_offset_lateral), mean_top3_closing_speed = mean(head(closing_speed[order(distance)], 3)), nearest_defender = defender_slot[which.min(distance)], .by = play_row ) # ``` ::: ::: ## The model Each play is either successful or it isn't, so I'm modelling the probability of success with logistic regression. The model weights the features, adds their contributions to a baseline, and turns the total into a probability. The model is written in the probabilistic programming languages [Stan](https://mc-stan.org/) (run from R) and [PyMC](https://www.pymc.io/) (Python). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"} ::: {.cell output.var='model'} ```{.stan .cell-code code-summary="Stan code · the whole model"} // Logistic regression on standardised football features. Two of the // features (yards needed and the nearest defender's cushion) arrive as natural // spline columns, built in R, so their effect can bend. data { int N; // plays the model learns from int K; // columns of the design matrix matrix[N, K] X; // standardised features and spline columns array[N] int y; // 1 = successful play int N_new; // plays or frames to score matrix[N_new, K] X_new; int prior_only; // 1 = ignore the outcomes } parameters { real alpha; // log-odds of success for an average play vector[K] beta; // change in log-odds per standard deviation } model { alpha ~ normal(0, 1); beta ~ normal(0, 0.35); if (!prior_only) { y ~ bernoulli_logit_glm(X, alpha, beta); } } generated quantities { // Pointwise log-likelihood, for leave-one-out cross-validation vector[N] log_lik; // Outcomes the model would expect to see, for predictive checks array[N] int y_rep = bernoulli_logit_rng(alpha + X * beta); // Probability of success for the plays or frames being scored vector[N_new] p_new = inv_logit(alpha + X_new * beta); for (n in 1:N) { log_lik[n] = bernoulli_logit_lpmf(y[n] | alpha + X[n] * beta); } } ``` ::: ## ![Python](/img/python-logo-only.svg){height="30"} ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code code-summary="Python code · the whole model"} # Logistic regression on standardised football features. Two of the # features (yards needed and the nearest defender's cushion) arrive as natural # spline columns (see the next chunk), so their effect can bend. def build_model(X, y, X_new=None): X_new = X.clear() if X_new is None else X_new coords = {"column": X.columns, "play": range(X.height), "new": range(X_new.height)} with pm.Model(coords=coords) as model: # Log-odds of success for an average play alpha = pm.Normal("alpha", 0, 1) # Change in log-odds per standard deviation beta = pm.Normal("beta", 0, 0.35, dims="column") pm.Bernoulli( "y", logit_p=alpha + pm.math.dot(X.to_numpy(), beta), observed=y, dims="play", ) # Probability of success for the plays or frames being scored pm.Deterministic( "p_new", pm.math.invlogit(alpha + pm.math.dot(X_new.to_numpy(), beta)), dims="new", ) return model ``` ::: ::: The model assumes seven of the nine features have a straight-line relationship with the log odds of success. For the other two (yards needed and cushion), I let the model fit a curve (using [splines](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YMl25iCCRew)). This is because going from 1 to 3 yards needed for a successful play is a big deal for a short pass, but 12 to 14 (same +2 yd difference) barely changes the odds (already low). When the nearest defender is close, an extra yard of space can be the difference between a tackle and a catch with room to run. When the defender's already far away or behind the receiver, another yard doesn't change much. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="R code · preparing the features for Stan"} # Turn play-level features into the design matrix the Stan model is fitted on. # # Everything learned from the training plays (centres, scales and spline knots) # is kept in a recipe and reused for any other plays or frames, so plays the # model has not seen never inform their own preprocessing. SPLINE_TERMS <- c(yards_needed = 4L, nearest_def_cushion = 3L) design_recipe <- function(train, features, spline_terms = SPLINE_TERMS) { linear <- setdiff(features, names(spline_terms)) bases <- imap( spline_terms, \(df, feature) splines::ns(train[[feature]], df = df) ) list( linear = linear, centre = map_dbl(train[linear], mean), scale = map_dbl(train[linear], sd), bases = bases, curve_centre = map(bases, colMeans), curve_scale = map(bases, \(basis) map_dbl(as_tibble(basis), sd)) ) } design_matrix <- function(plays, recipe) { linear <- plays[recipe$linear] |> as.matrix() |> scale(center = recipe$centre, scale = recipe$scale) curves <- imap(recipe$bases, \(basis, feature) { curve <- predict(basis, plays[[feature]]) |> scale( center = recipe$curve_centre[[feature]], scale = recipe$curve_scale[[feature]] ) colnames(curve) <- str_c(feature, "_curve", seq_len(ncol(curve))) curve }) reduce(curves, cbind, .init = linear) } stan_data <- function(train, recipe, new = NULL, prior_only = FALSE) { X <- design_matrix(train, recipe) X_new <- if (is.null(new)) { X[0, , drop = FALSE] } else { design_matrix(new, recipe) } list( N = nrow(X), K = ncol(X), X = X, y = as.integer(train$success), N_new = nrow(X_new), X_new = X_new, prior_only = as.integer(prior_only) ) } # Centres, scales and curve shapes are learned from the training plays recipe <- design_recipe(plays, final_features) ``` ::: ## ![Python](/img/python-logo-only.svg){height="30"} ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code code-summary="Python code · preparing the features for the model"} # Turn play-level features into the design matrix the model is fitted on. # # Everything learned from the training plays (centres, scales and spline knots) # is kept in a recipe and reused for any other plays or frames, so plays the # model has not seen never inform their own preprocessing. SPLINE_TERMS = {"yards_needed": 4, "nearest_def_cushion": 3} def natural_spline(x, df): """A natural cubic spline for x, Python's usual stand-in for R's splines::ns(x, df). Centring the columns leaves the baseline to alpha.""" spline = f"cr(x, df={df}, constraints='center') - 1" return model_matrix(spline, pl.DataFrame({"x": x})).model_spec def spline_basis(spline, x): """The spline's columns at x. Beyond the outer knots the curve carries on as a straight line.""" return np.asarray(spline.get_model_matrix(pl.DataFrame({"x": x}))) def design_recipe(train, features, spline_terms=SPLINE_TERMS): linear = [feature for feature in features if feature not in spline_terms] splines = { feature: natural_spline(train[feature], df) for feature, df in spline_terms.items() } curves = { feature: spline_basis(spline, train[feature]) for feature, spline in splines.items() } return { "linear": linear, "centre": {feature: train[feature].mean() for feature in linear}, "scale": {feature: train[feature].std() for feature in linear}, "splines": splines, "curve_centre": { feature: curve.mean(axis=0) for feature, curve in curves.items() }, "curve_scale": { feature: curve.std(axis=0, ddof=1) for feature, curve in curves.items() }, } def design_matrix(plays, recipe): linear = plays.select( (pl.col(feature) - recipe["centre"][feature]) / recipe["scale"][feature] for feature in recipe["linear"] ) curves = [] for feature, spline in recipe["splines"].items(): curve = ( spline_basis(spline, plays[feature]) - recipe["curve_centre"][feature] ) / (recipe["curve_scale"][feature]) names = [f"{feature}_curve{i}" for i in range(1, curve.shape[1] + 1)] curves.append(pl.DataFrame(curve, schema=names, orient="row")) return pl.concat([linear, *curves], how="horizontal") # Centres, scales and curve shapes are learned from the training plays recipe = design_recipe(plays, final_features) # The training plays as the model sees them X = design_matrix(plays, recipe) y = plays["success"].to_numpy() ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Prior predictive check and simulation-based calibration (technical details) **Do the priors make sense?** Bayesian models like this one need priors representing our beliefs about the distribution of plausible parameter values. Because thinking about parameters and understanding their impact on observed outcomes isn't natural to most psychologically well-adjusted humans, it's good practice to simulate outcome data using parameter values drawn from our prior distributions. This way we can see if those choices of priors generate outcome values within the realms of reality. The no-skill reference is the overall success rate (0.59). - **ROC-AUC** (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve): the chance that a randomly picked successful play is rated higher than a randomly picked unsuccessful one. 0.5 is a coin flip and 1 is perfect. - **Accuracy**: the share of plays called correctly, counting anything rated 50% or more as a call of success. - **Brier score**: the average squared gap between the predicted probability and what happened (1 for a successful play, 0 otherwise). It rewards probabilities that are confident and right. Lower is better, and always guessing the average scores 0.24. ::: The headline metric in the CNN post is [PR-AUC](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4jRBRDbJemM&t=824s). The logistic regression model scores **0.827** against the CNN's **0.793**. This doesn't mean "regression beats neural networks" (because often it won't), but on this problem I didn't have to give up any predictive ability to get a model that is more transparent about what contributes to a given prediction. This compares the two approaches as a whole. My model also includes receiver depth relative to the line of scrimmage, which wasn't included in the CNN's inputs. Some of the improvement is from that extra context. ### Can you believe the probabilities? If a model says 70% probability of success, plays like that should succeed about 70% of the time. Experts can hold it up against the film and challenge it until it's refined enough to trust. ## The limits Every play the model learned from is a moment a QB chose to throw. The earlier frames in the videos are moments the QB chose not to, probably for reasons the features can't see (the dashed box in the [DAG above](#not-instructions)). So the number could be a bit off before the throw, and its interval doesn't widen to warn you. Bridgewater might have held on to the ball through the peak above 80% because of something the model can't see. To summarise the limitations of my model (and of any model of this data, short of assumptions I don't think hold): - **It isn't causal.** It describes what tends to go with success ([these are not instructions](#not-instructions)). It can't tell you what would happen if a player did something different. - **It only knows about completed passes.** It never saw a pass that was dropped, missed its target, intercepted, blocked, etc. So its number assumes the catch is made and risky throws look better than they are. - **It knows nothing about the actual throw.** The features describe the space around the receiver, not the path the ball has to travel. A moment it rates highly might have a defensive lineman standing in the throwing lane with hands up. - **Before the throw, it's answering a different question.** It learned from moments quarterbacks chose to throw, not moments they held on. [See above](#not-instructions). - **It's 3,228 completed short passes** from the first half of two seasons. ## The wrap I wanted to see whether compressing the information from complex, high-dimensional tracking inputs into features representing football concepts would cost much in predictive performance. In this case it didn't. That doesn't mean neural networks are the wrong tool. If nobody knows how to describe what matters, letting a flexible model find patterns in the raw data is a good approach, and it's probably a sensible place to start with tracking data. What I found is that this outcome could be described well by nine features covering six football concepts. Once that's true, the simple model is the easier one to inspect, question, and trust. It also shows that football knowledge can go *into* a model, not just come out of it. Yards needed, the feature most strongly associated with success, is just the success rule applied to down and distance. The CNN had to learn that rule; I could just tell the model. It could be applied practically in film review with players. Why does the model like one situation more than another? Does that match what they see? If not, what has it missed? It'd also be interesting to see which players consistently succeed more or less often than the model expects (implications on player evaluation and scouting). For real use though, I'd want a version trained on every throw (incompletions and interceptions included), not just the completed ones, and ideally one that also models when quarterbacks choose to throw. ::: callout-note ## Reproduce this - **The analysis.** Everything in this post runs from the files in [`data-public/`](https://github.com/mitchhenderson/mitchhenderson.dev/tree/main/posts/2026-10-19-nfl-interpretability-vs-predictive-power/data-public), next to the post's source on GitHub.
